theme: Naaman healed; Gehazi’s greed; the Syrian siege
readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 5:1-6:33. Naaman the Syrian is healed of leprosy, Gehazi’s greed is judged, and Elisha is surrounded by an army and sees a greater one. Read the story of Naaman as a picture of grace that humbles.
settingTheScene: Elisha’s ministry extends to foreigners. Naaman is a commander of the Syrian army, Israel’s enemy, and a leper. Through the witness of a captured Israelite girl, he comes to the prophet. These chapters include one of the Bible’s best stories of grace, followed by a sad story of greed, and the account of the Syrian siege of Samaria.
observation: A little Israelite girl says to Naaman’s wife, “Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy” (5:3).
Elisha sends a messenger: “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored” (5:10).
Naaman is angry: “Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me” (5:11).
His servants say, “If the prophet had commanded you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?” (5:13).
“His flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean” (5:14).
Naaman says, “Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel” (5:15).
Gehazi takes a gift Elisha refused, and Naaman’s leprosy clings to him (5:20-27).
“Do not fear, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (6:16).
interpretation:
The story begins with a nameless girl. She is a captive and a servant, with every reason to be bitter. Yet she wishes her master’s health and points him to the prophet. A small voice of faith makes a large difference. God uses the unnoticed.

Naaman comes with horses, chariots, silver, gold, and a letter from a king. He expects a spectacle. Elisha does not even come out. He sends a messenger with a plain instruction: wash in the Jordan. Naaman is furious. The muddy Jordan seems beneath him. He wanted to be healed on his own terms, in a way that honored his status. It is a picture of pride that resists grace. His servants help him see sense: “If he had commanded you to do some great thing, would you not have done it? How much more, when he says to you, Wash, and be clean?” The simplicity of the remedy was the offense.

When he humbles himself and obeys, he is healed and his skin becomes like a child’s. He confesses the LORD as the only God. It is a conversion. He asks to take two mule-loads of earth, so that he can worship the LORD in Syria.

The contrast with Gehazi is sharp. Gehazi, who has been with the prophet and seen miracles, sees an opportunity to profit from grace. He lies to get the gift. The leprosy of Naaman passes to him. The outsider is cleansed, and the insider is judged. Proximity to God’s work is no substitute for faith.

Chapter 6 gives a different scene. The Syrian army surrounds Elisha’s city. His servant is terrified. Elisha prays, and the servant’s eyes are opened to see the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. The unseen world is real. And Elisha’s unusual response to the captured Syrian army is to feed them and send them home. “And the Syrians no more came on raids.” Kindness did what swords could not.
connection: Jesus used Naaman’s story in his sermon at Nazareth (Luke 4:27), pointing out that God’s mercy reaches the Gentiles. Baptism is a washing that seems simple but is a sign of cleansing by grace (Titus 3:5). Romans 12:20-21 says to feed your enemy and overcome evil with good. Jesus told his disciples, “Do not be afraid, little flock” (Luke 12:32), and Revelation 5:11 shows the heavenly host surrounding the throne. 1 Timothy 6:10 warns of the love of money, as seen in Gehazi.
application:
Ask where pride keeps you from receiving grace in a simple form.

Think about the “little girl” in your life who points you to God. Thank them.

Pray for the eyes of your heart to be opened, as Elisha prayed for his servant.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to humble your pride so that you can receive his grace in the simple way he gives it.
Thank him for the little ones who point to him.
Ask him to open your eyes to see his armies around you.
